1:
The single verse carries the whole question of authorship, and the witnesses divide. reformed Gill has no doubt: the author is the Judas who was one of the twelve, whose other name was Lebbaeus and surname Thaddaeus, the name itself Judah, from a word signifying to praise or confess. Calvin agrees that servant is used not as the title belongs to all the godly but with respect to the apostleship, those with a public office committed to them being peculiarly so called; and he draws a double sense from it, that God bestows the office and the holder faithfully performs it — many boast to be what they are far from being, and we ought to examine whether the reality answers it. grammatical-historical Barnes reconstructs it from the catalogues: the tenth place in one list is Lebbeus surnamed Thaddeus, that name is absent from the other where the tenth place is Simon called Zelotes, and the same evangelist afterwards names Judas the brother of James, so the two are supposed to be one man. The James meant cannot be the elder, slain by Herod too early and better identified as the brother of John, but the one still living in Jerusalem, known besides as the brother of the Lord. Of Jude himself only one thing is preserved in the Gospels: the question he put on the eve of the crucifixion, how his Master would manifest himself to them and not to the world (John 14:22). wesleyan-arminian Clarke reaches the opposite conclusion from the silence. The writer assumes neither the title of apostle nor that of brother of the Lord; had he been both, he would hardly have called himself simply the brother of James without saying so. The evangelist gives the apostle Jude that description only to distinguish him from the traitor, and the writer could have had no motive for distinguishing himself from a man dead by his own hand many years before.

On the title itself they converge, and diverge again over the participles. puritan-evangelical Henry observes that the same names may be common to the best and worst of persons, this Judas a sincere disciple where the other was the betrayer, and that he might have claimed kindred to Christ after the flesh but glories in being his servant — a greater honour than kinship, many of his natural kindred having perished, not from want of affection in him but from unbelief in themselves. The apostles, he adds, were servants before they were apostles and servants still, so all pretension to lordly dominion in Christ’s ministers is out of place. Wesley makes the word the highest glory angel or man can aspire to, and marks the covenantal shift: under the old covenant servant suited the spirit of fear and bondage, but once the Son came to redeem those under the law it meant one who, having the Spirit of adoption, is made free by the Son, so that servanthood is the fruit and perfection of sonship. He notes that the epistle’s conclusion exactly answers its introduction, and that both the spring and the accomplishment of salvation are named at the outset lest any reader be discouraged by the terrible things to follow. Robertson holds the grammar open at three points: whether the word rendered called is a substantive or stands in the predicate, two participles intervening; that there is no parallel to this use of the preposition with the verb for loving; and that the last participle may be dative or instrumental, so the readers are kept for Jesus Christ or else by him. Calvin takes the same clauses doctrinally: calling is nothing but the effect of eternal election, men never come to God until he draws them, and being profane in themselves they have their holiness in God, who sanctifies by regeneration. The reading beloved he judges corrupt, found in but a few copies.
2:
The salutation is short and the notes on it expand its three nouns. reformed Calvin observes that mercy stands here nearly where grace stands in the other apostolic greetings, and offers a refinement: grace is properly the effect of mercy, since there is no other reason why God embraced us in love but that he pitied our miseries. He then asks whether the love is God’s toward men or men’s toward one another, and judges it more consistent to take peace and love as God’s, since the mercy plainly is — though the other sense is not unsuitable, that God would kindle mutual love among them. Gill distributes the words across the persons: mercy from the Father who sanctified them, shown in the covenant, in the provision and mission of Christ, in redemption, forgiveness and regeneration; and peace from Christ in whom they were preserved. Multiplication he takes for an enlarged view and a fresh application, needed under desertions, under temptations and afflictions, and after falling into sin. grammatical-historical Barnes notes the form is not quite that of the other apostles but is equally expressive, and reads the three as the choicest blessings that could be conferred — mercy in pardon and acceptance, peace with God and men and in one’s conscience and in the prospect of death, love to God and the brethren and all the world — then asks what blessing these do not include. Robertson notes only the mood: the verb is an optative, exactly as in the two letters of Peter. wesleyan-arminian Clarke supplies the reason for the first word: even the best have no merit, and must receive every blessing and grace in the way of mercy.

The purpose of the letter is stated next, and the witnesses disagree about how it was arrived at. Clarke thinks the writer had first purposed a general account of the nature and design of the Gospel, then changed his mind on seeing the danger from false teachers. Barnes traces a slower process: affection prompted him to write, the general subject was necessarily the common salvation, and only on reflecting what their peculiar dangers required did he settle on this exhortation. Calvin separates the two clauses instead — though Jude was inclined and anxious to write, a necessity compelled him, because they were already assailed and needed preparing to fight; and since necessity adds strong stimulants, the preface was as though he had blown a trumpet to wake them from their torpor. Calvin also rejects the copies that add your to the salvation, since Jude makes it common to them and to himself: what we say is vain if we speak of salvation to others while having no real knowledge of it, so he professes himself here an experimental teacher. puritan-evangelical Henry takes common in the widest sense, as offered sincerely to all mankind to whom notice of it reaches, none excluded but those who obstinately exclude themselves — and adds that none should discourage themselves over hidden decrees, since God’s decrees are dark but his covenants are plain. On what is to be contended for he is emphatic: it must really be the Christian faith, not the discriminating badges of this or the other party, nor anything later than the inspired writings; nothing can be added and nothing detracted, and here we should abide, for a step further leaves us in danger of being entangled or seduced. Barnes and Robertson both note that the verb belongs to the Grecian games and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament — a little additional striving added to a word already strong — though Barnes restricts the contention to argument, reasoning and holding fast. Wesley adds the qualification the others leave implicit: earnestly, yet humbly, meekly and lovingly, since otherwise the contention will only hurt the cause, if not destroy the soul.
4:
The intruders are introduced by a verb of stealth, and every witness dwells there. grammatical-historical Robertson glosses it as slipping in secretly by a side door, a compound found nowhere else in the New Testament, and marks the keynote word, ungodly, returning at the height of the argument. Barnes reads the stealth morally: they had not come by open avowal of their real sentiments, but professed to teach the Christian religion while denying its fundamentals and professed holiness while living scandalous lives. reformed Calvin makes the point structural. Satan is always an enemy to the godly, but Jude describes the state of things at that time, and a faithful pastor ought to consider what the present state of the Church requires, so as to accommodate his doctrine to its wants. The word denotes an indirect and stealthy insinuation, for Satan sows his tares in the night while the husbandmen sleep; and the evil is intestine, since he raises up men out of the flock itself, who for that reason creep in the more easily. Gill lists the doors they came through — into private houses, into the churches as members, into the ministry without being called, and into the affections of the saints — and explains why no names or number are given: to stir the saints to self-examination, to diligence in finding such men out, to vigour in opposing them, and to care in nipping error in the bud. He adds that Peter and Paul foretold their coming, while Jude speaks of them as already present, so vigilance was now required rather than expectation.

The hardest clause says they were of old set down for this condemnation, and the readings run apart. wesleyan-arminian Clarke takes the verb in its public sense — long ago proscribed and condemned openly, a usage he says is common in the Greek writers — and calls it as ridiculous as it is absurd to look in such words for a decree of eternal reprobation, a doctrine as far from the writer’s mind as from that of him in whose name he wrote. Barnes reaches nearly the same place by lexical caution: the adverb means long ago without determining how long, so the reference may be any remote period; and while it might cover eternity if that were known on other grounds, it may be doubted whether this word would have been chosen, and no eternal ordination can be proved from it. Wesley and Robertson point forward instead, taking the of old to reach back as far as Enoch, whose prophecy stands later in the chapter. Calvin alone keeps the decree in view, though he too locates the reference in prophecy: the metaphor is drawn from the eternal counsel of God being called a book, and Jude’s object was to keep the novelty of the thing from distressing anyone, since if these men were long ago ordained the Church is tried only according to God’s infallible counsel. What they did with grace all describe alike. Calvin says they abused it so as to take an impure liberty in sinning, when grace appeared for the contrary purpose, and calls nothing more pestilential than men who make the grace of Christ a cloak for lasciviousness — noting, with an eye to his own controversies, that the same charge is laid against those who teach that salvation comes by mercy alone. Clarke has them making the grace of God a covering for crimes, on the pretence that men may sin safely where grace abounds, and Wesley that they turned the grace revealed in the gospel into an occasion of more abandoned wickedness. On the closing title Clarke and Robertson agree against the received text: the word for God is absent from many manuscripts and was probably a gloss, so one person and not two is denied here, the single article carrying the phrase over to Christ alone.
5:
Three examples follow, and the first question is why. wesleyan-arminian Clarke says the word rendered once has greatly puzzled interpreters, since it can mean one time as opposed to twice, or altogether and perfectly; he takes the latter, so the readers are already thoroughly instructed. reformed Calvin offers two accounts and prefers the bolder: either Jude excuses himself lest he seem to teach the ignorant, or he declares openly that he brings nothing new, so what follows may gain the more credit. The use of God’s word, he adds, is not only to teach what we could not otherwise know but to rouse us to meditate on what we understand, and not let us grow torpid in a cold knowledge. Gill agrees that they had known it perfectly, lest the writer be thought to address the ignorant. On the first example they converge. grammatical-historical Barnes marks the adverb as literally the second time: first they were delivered, second destroyed, so the fact of rescue did not prevent destruction — and men who seem delivered from sin will not be spared if they live wickedly. Robertson notes that all rescued from Egypt perished but two, and that this example is absent from Peter’s parallel letter. Calvin puts the weight on unbelief, the fountain of all evils, since every sin recorded of them came of refusing to be ruled by God’s word; where there is the subjection of faith, obedience appears in all the duties of life. puritan-evangelical Henry states the moral flatly: outward privileges, profession and apparent conversion could not secure those who turned aside in unbelief; they had miracles as daily bread, and perished still. Wesley adds that it was the far greater part of the very people God had saved, so none should presume on past mercies as if now out of danger.

The second example draws the sharpest notes. Gill has the angels created in perfect holiness, sons of God comparable to the morning stars, until one sinned and drew the rest after him. Clarke insists that from what they fell, or for what crime, we do not know — pride is generally supposed but this is mere conjecture — while one thing is certain, that they were on probation, capable of standing or falling, as Adam was. Barnes reads the words as rank and dwelling-place, and thinks the phrasing may suggest they grew dissatisfied with their abode and preferred to change it, though the cause is unknown; and he denies the clause proves their punishment eternal, since it says only that they are kept in a dark prison until the final trial. Calvin argues from the greater to the less: if God punished the defection of celestial powers so dreadfully, he will not forgive ours — and he refuses to imagine a place where the devils are shut up, since wherever they go they drag their own chains with them. Wesley draws the inference about God rather than the angels: they came holy from his hands, or God made what was evil, and being holy they were beloved; that he loves them no more, and that love and displeasure fall on the same work of his hands, is because he changes not. On the third example one small phrase divides them. Barnes canvasses four and settles on the cities round about Sodom, rejecting the angels and the false teachers, since that would have Sodom copying an example set long after; Robertson takes it in exactly the sense Barnes rejects, of the fallen angels; Calvin refers it neither to Israel nor the angels but to the inhabitants of the cities themselves. Clarke allows the fire to be called eternal in two senses, the endless punishment of the inhabitants or the irreversible destruction of the cities, whose ground is now a lake; Calvin and Wesley agree that the visible burning was a type of a much heavier punishment.
8:
The epithet given to the intruders is disputed at the word itself. grammatical-historical Barnes points out that filthy was supplied by the translators with no good reason: the Greek means simply to dream, and is applied to men whose doctrines stand to truth as dreams to good sense, being the fruits of mere imagination and foolish fancy. wesleyan-arminian Clarke defends the supplement, taking it of self-pollution with its train of cursed effects on body, soul and spirit, and finds the reading confirmed by the next clause about defiling the flesh. reformed Gill spreads his net over both and adds a third: the words may be taken of teachers who professed to interpret dreams, of nocturnal pollution, a sense two versions support, or of claimed intelligence by dream; and figuratively of the doctrines themselves, since false doctrines are dreams and their teachers dreamers — among which he numbers whatever opposes the Trinity, contradicts the deity of Christ, or cries up the power and righteousness of human nature. Calvin takes the metaphor for stupor: they abandoned themselves to filth which the most wicked abhor, as though sleep took away shame and consciousness — though he allows the word may allude to the old false prophets who taught what they pretended to see in dreams, and thinks it not improbable these men claimed supernatural dreams, since otherwise errors so gross could hardly have deceived. Calvin also finds an architecture the others miss: the three charges answer the three examples in order — defiling of flesh to the Sodomites, despising of dominion to the angels, reviling of dignities to Israel, whose unbelief showed itself in opposing the power given to Moses. Robertson reads the comparison more simply, as pointing back only to the cities of the plain, while Clarke maps it onto persons rather than sins: as unbelieving as Israel, as rebellious as the angels, as impure as the Sodomites.

What is despised and reviled is the second question. puritan-evangelical Henry gives three answers himself. Taken of civil power, the men are of a disturbed mind and seditious spirit who forget that the powers that be are ordained of God, so in blaspheming magistrates they blaspheme God. Taken of religion, they despise the dominion of conscience, make a jest of it and would banish it from the world, and despise the word of God which is its rule, allowing the divine will to go for little except as they have first imposed their own sense of it on everyone about them. Taken a third way, the dignities are the people of God themselves, of whom it was said, touch not mine anointed — religion and its serious professors having always been evil spoken of. Calvin holds to the civil sense and turns it against his contemporaries: the second clause shows them seditious men who sought anarchy so that, loosed from fear of the laws, they might sin more freely; and the two go nearly always together, since those who abandon themselves to iniquity wish also to abolish all order. He compares them to the fanatics of his own day, who not only grumble at being restrained by magistrates but declaim furiously against all government, call the power of the sword profane and opposed to godliness, and reject all kings and magistrates from the Church of God. Clarke says the same in fewer words: they set all government at nought, will come under no restraint, despise all law and wish to live as they list, misrepresenting every divine and civil institution. Wesley alone denies the civil reference outright. The apostle does not seem to speak of worldly dignities, he says, for those these men had in admiration for the sake of gain; the dignities meant are holy men, honourable before God for the purity of their lives and the greatness of their labours, grossly vilified by those who turned the grace of God into lasciviousness.
9:
This is the verse that has cost the epistle most. grammatical-historical Barnes says it has given more perplexity than any other part of the letter, and that the difficulty has led some to reject the epistle: nothing of the kind is in the Old Testament, and the story looks like a mere Jewish fable. He examines the proposals in turn. Some refer it to the vision where Satan stands at the high priest’s right hand to resist him — but only the words the Lord rebuke thee are common to the two; Michael is not named there, the body of Moses is not mentioned, and the reason for Satan’s resistance is given and concerns the priest’s consecration. Others suppose the material came from apocryphal books current at the time, used not as conceding their truth but to refute from books his opponents valued — against which Barnes objects that Jude seems to refer to it as fact. Robertson reports the same two, adds a rabbinical comment on the burial notice, and concludes none of them quite meets the facts; early Christian writers, he notes, said outright that Jude was quoting an apocryphal book. reformed Calvin admits the charge and denies its force. Since the Jews then had much from the traditions of the fathers, he sees nothing unreasonable in saying Jude referred to what had been handed down for ages; many puerilities have borne the name of tradition, as in his own day the silly dotages of the monks, but that is no reason why there should not also have been historical facts never committed to writing. wesleyan-arminian Wesley takes the same ground more briefly: it does not appear whether the writer learned this by revelation or from ancient tradition, and it suffices that the things were true and acknowledged as such by those to whom he wrote. Clarke is franker still: what this means, or whence it was drawn, he cannot tell.

On the identity of Michael they scatter. Gill argues that no created angel is meant but an eternal one, Christ himself: the name signifies who is as God, and none is like God but the Son; the title of archangel suits the head of all principality and power; and what is said elsewhere of Michael, the great Prince with angels at his command, agrees with none but Christ. Clarke arrives near the same place by another road, observing that archangel is never plural in the sacred writings, so there can properly be only one, head of all the angelic orders, just as the word for the great enemy is never plural; and many, he notes, understand the Lord Jesus by him. Wesley refuses to settle it: the word occurs only once more in Scripture, so whether there is one archangel or more cannot be determined. Calvin treats him as one angel among myriads, chosen for this business as God pleased, and reads it as an argument from the greater to the less: Michael dared not speak more severely against Satan than to deliver him over to God to be restrained, while these men load with reproaches the powers God has adorned with peculiar honours. What was contended for divides them too. Calvin and Wesley keep to the corpse: Moses was buried by the Lord and his grave concealed, lest the Jews bring out his body to promote superstition, so Satan would naturally try to make the place known — Calvin adding that Satan has in almost every age endeavoured to make the bodies of the saints into idols. Clarke reports instead a reading that takes the body of Moses for the Jewish Church and state, whose destruction Satan contended for, as the Christian Church is called the body of Christ; he calls it the most likely he has seen, the more so because among the Hebrews the word for body often stands for the thing itself.
10:
What the intruders rail at turns on the word know. reformed Gill supplies four candidates: angels, known only by revelation and blasphemed either by ascribing too much to them or by saying things unworthy of them; civil magistrates, whose nature and use they were ignorant of; the ministers of the Gospel, whose usefulness they did not acknowledge; and the Scriptures, denied to be the word of God or covered with false glosses. grammatical-historical Barnes draws the contrast as one of range: their knowledge was confined to what they had in common with the brutes — instinct, appetite, sensual pleasure — and never rose to the contemplation of the higher things against which they used only reproach. There are multitudes of such men, he says: they do not understand high and holy objects, but they can rail at them. wesleyan-arminian Clarke applies it to government again: they do not understand the origin and utility of civil order, and revile the thing that protects their own persons and property. Calvin puts the emphasis on audacity: having no taste for anything but what was gross and beastly, they did not perceive what was worthy of honour, and added audacity to madness by condemning what was above their comprehension; and in what they did feel they kept no moderation, gorging themselves like swine in mud, since instinct alone rules brute animals while reason ought to govern men and bridle their appetites. Wesley marks the asymmetry in a line: the things of God they cannot know, having no spiritual senses, and the natural things they do know they abuse into occasions of sin.

The woe that follows is a departure, and the witnesses notice it. Wesley observes that of all the apostles Jude alone, and in this single place, denounces a woe. Gill offers three readings of it — a commiseration of their case, a denunciation of deserved punishment, or a prediction of what would befall them. Calvin denies it is imprecation at all: Jude did not so much call down evil on them as remind them what sort of end awaited them, and did it lest they should carry others with them to perdition. Ellicott hears in it an echo of the denunciations in the Gospels, and explains the past tenses that follow as the writer placing himself at the moment when these men reap their sins, the punishment being so certain that he treats it as already come — a point Barnes makes independently. On the first of the three the readings divide. Clarke takes the way of Cain to be hatred of the brethren, since haters of their brethren are murderers, and adds that by false doctrine they destroy souls. Barnes lists pride, hatred of religion, restlessness under the restraints of virtue and envy that others were more favoured, leading at last to the spirit that produced the murder. Calvin makes Cain the man who, ungrateful to God and perverting his worship, forfeited his birthright. Ellicott brushes all of these aside as needlessly far-fetched: Cain was simply the first great criminal, the first to outrage the laws of nature, and sensuality is always selfish but by no means always malignant. He alone sees the triplet as a structure rather than a list, matching the three names to the three earlier examples in order — Cain like the men of Sodom outraging nature, Balaam like the impure angels despising God’s sovereignty, Korah like the unbelieving Israelites speaking evil of dignities. On the middle name Robertson, Wesley and Calvin agree that the verb means poured out, a torrent without banks; Ellicott lists three possible renderings of the clause and prefers the received one, taking the allusion to lie on the surface as running counter to God’s will from interested motives.
12:
The first word of the verse is contested in the lexicon. grammatical-historical Barnes observes that the word here is not the one used in the parallel epistle: it means a rock by or in the sea, a cliff on which vessels wreck or a hidden rock on which they strand unawares, so the idea is not that these men were blemishes at the feasts but that they were as dangerous in the church as hidden rocks in the ocean, causing others to make shipwreck of their faith. Robertson gives the same gloss, rocks covered by the water. reformed Gill keeps the older sense, spots or blemishes, alluding to spots in garments or faces or sacrifices; Wesley says simply blemishes. What the feasts were divides them more sharply. Gill, Clarke and Calvin all take them for the love-feasts of the primitive Christians: Gill describes them as begun and ended with prayer and singing, kept with frugality to refresh the poor saints, and quickly abused by intemperance and by excluding the very poor they were meant for; Clarke traces them to the fourth century, when a council prohibited them, and notes their revival in his own day; Calvin calls them feasts the faithful held to testify brotherly unity, disgraced by men who crammed themselves at the church’s cost. Barnes stands alone against all three. There is no evidence, he says, unless it be here, that such celebrations had apostolic sanction; the supposition is not needed, since the words are met by referring them to the Lord’s Supper, itself in every sense a festival of love; and the later prevalence of the custom is accounted for from Jewish festivals and the heathen practice of feasting upon a sacrifice. Clarke and Robertson note that some early copies read deceits instead of love-feasts, Clarke suspecting the change was made to avoid the conclusion that a church holding such men must be very corrupt.

The metaphors that follow are read as one mounting series. Clarke expounds the clouds from the arid countries where a cloud is delightful as a token of rain, until sudden winds disperse it and the husbandman’s hope is cut off: these men have the form and office of teachers of righteousness and distil no showers, because they have none. Calvin compresses two of the parallel similitudes into one and finds the series aimed at vain ostentation. Robertson notes that where the parallel epistle has springs without water and mists driven by storm, this writer has clouds borne round in circles, a powerful picture of disappointed hopes. On the twice dead Calvin gives two accounts: a proverbial way of saying altogether dead, or dead while professing Judaism and dead again after the gospel. Wesley says dead in sin, by nature and then by apostasy, and takes plucked up by the roots to mean incapable of reviving. On the last figure the astronomy is in dispute. Barnes allows planets, comets or meteors, the point being that stars serve the mariner only because regular, and these teachers can be depended on for nothing. Wesley reads them as planets, which shine for a time but have no light of their own. Clarke denies the planets outright: their motions are perfectly steady, and their seeming to advance, stand still and go backward is only an effect of being viewed from the earth; what is meant is uncertain meteors, dancing in a darkness of their own making and leading simple souls astray. Robertson reports comets or shooting stars as commonly suggested. Calvin turns the figure on the sects of his own day, who despise common language and form an exotic idiom, carrying their disciples above heaven at one moment and falling to beastly errors the next — and concludes that the simplicity of Scripture ought to be studied with more care, lest by reasoning more refinedly than is right we draw men not to heaven but into labyrinths.
14:
The quotation raises the same question as the dispute over Moses’ body. grammatical-historical Barnes states his position carefully: there is no clear evidence the writer quoted from any book extant in his time, the apocryphal work bearing the patriarch’s name cannot be certainly dated before him, and both may have drawn on a common tradition, since among the multitude of Jewish traditions some were doubtless true. No one can prove this one was not; no one can show that an inspired writer might not be led to select a true prophecy from a mass of traditions; so the quotation is no argument against the inspiration of the epistle. He adds that the style bears the marks of a quotation, being less terse than the writer’s own, and that the substance is what the age called for, the man being good in a corrupt generation and likely to be reproached by hard speeches himself. reformed Calvin takes the prophecy to have been unwritten rather than drawn from an apocryphal book, thinks the book so called was probably a forgery occasioned by this reference, and explains why an ancient testimony was preferred to a written prophet’s: the writer wished to repeat from the oldest antiquity what the Spirit had pronounced, and says expressly that the man was seventh from Adam to commend the prophecy’s age, since it existed before the flood. wesleyan-arminian Clarke dismisses the book as apocryphal and will not burden his page with extracts, though he grants it was known early and quoted by the fathers; and he offers a way round the difficulty, that the verb may mean no more than preached, since the man doubtless reproved the ungodliness of his own times. Wesley leaves it open between an ancient book, a tradition and a revelation. Robertson alone takes the harder line: if the verb has its ordinary meaning, the writer terms the Book of Enoch inspired, the words quoted being a combination of passages from it. On the ten thousand Calvin includes angels and the faithful, since both will adorn the tribunal, and reads the number as comfort: the multitude of the ungodly may not overwhelm the children of God like a violent sea, since the Lord will one day collect his own, part dwelling unseen in heaven and part hidden here under a great mass of chaff.

The verse that follows is harsh, and each notices it differently. Clarke reports that it is loaded with various readings, the manuscripts at little agreement on its phraseology, one pronoun being probably spurious, one noun often omitted and one word supplied by the translators; and he corrects a claim that the prophecy opened with a known formula of excommunication, the words being not Hebrew but Syriac and meaning simply that the Lord is coming. Calvin sees a want of order rather than of text: judgment is named first and the conviction of the ungodly second, the reverse of the actual sequence — but this corresponds with numberless passages of Scripture, where the final action is put first and afterwards what leads to it. Barnes takes the disputed verb in a sense the modern reader will miss. We now use convince of satisfying a man’s own mind, a conviction produced by argument and not necessarily followed by any sentence; but that is clearly not the sense here, for the purpose of the coming is not to persuade men, though the wicked will see their lives were wrong, but to pronounce sentence on the evidence. Robertson counts the refrain instead: some form of the word for ungodliness sounds four times in one verse. Gill enumerates the all who are judged — quick and dead, small and great, rich and poor, sheep and goats — and Wesley marks a gradation, a sinner being bad but the ungodly who sin without fear worse, adding that the man who spoke here looked beyond the flood.
16:
Two words open the verse, and the readings differ over whom each aims at. wesleyan-arminian Wesley makes the cleanest division: murmurers against men, complainers against their own fate and so against God, walking after their own desires with regard to themselves. grammatical-historical Barnes glosses the second word literally, as finding fault with one’s own lot, and observes that nothing is more common — the poor complain that they are not rich, the sick that they are not well, the bereaved that they are deprived of friends, those in humble life that their lot was not cast among the great; and he names the opposed virtue, contentment, calling it of inestimable value. Clarke has them grumbling at all men and all things, finding fault with God and every providential dispensation, making and governing worlds in their own way, persons whom neither God nor man can please. reformed Gill divides the murmuring as Wesley does but fills both sides out: against God, his being and perfections and sovereignty, his purposes, his providence and the unequal distribution of things, and especially the doctrines of free grace; and against men, the magistrates who restrain them, the ministers whose gifts they envy, and all their neighbours besides. Calvin traces the temper to its root: those who indulge depraved lusts are hard to please and never satisfied, so they murmur however kindly good men treat them — and by the very indulgence they walk in they make their lot worse and give themselves fresh occasion to grumble. puritan-evangelical Henry states the matter as character: such men are angry at everything that happens and never pleased with their own condition, as not thinking it good enough for them; and he adds that those who please their sinful appetites are the most prone to yield to ungovernable passions.

The second half of the verse joins two things they find incongruous. Calvin sets them side by side: their proud language shows them boasting of themselves, while their servile submission for gain shows how mean they were in disposition; and this inconsistency is commonly seen in unprincipled men. Where there is no one to check their insolence, or nothing standing in their way, their pride is intolerable and they imperiously arrogate everything to themselves; but they meanly flatter those whom they fear, and from whom they expect some advantage. Barnes puts it as a failure of justice in esteem: they did not appreciate men according to their real worth, but paid particular attention to one class, the rich and the great, to promote their own selfish ends. Clarke turns it on his own profession and does not spare it. These are time-servers and flatterers, he says, who pretend to be astonished at the greatness, goodness, learning and wisdom of rich men, hoping to acquire money, influence, power and friends; all the flatterers of the rich are of this kind, and especially those who profess to be ministers of the Gospel and who, for a more advantageous living, will soothe the rich even in their sins. With such persons a rich man is everything, and if he have but a grain of grace his piety is extolled to the skies. He adds that he has known several ministers of this character and wishes them all to read the verse. Wesley says the same in eight words, that they admire and commend men only for what they can get from them. Robertson supplies the philology: the word for murmurers is an imitative formation, the word for complainers is rare and compounded of complaining and one’s lot, and the phrase for showing respect of persons is a Hebraism, the same idiom that the Old Testament uses when it forbids partiality in judgment.
17:
The turn to the readers begins with memory. grammatical-historical Barnes notes the close similarity to the parallel passage in Peter, standing in the same connection and couched almost in the same words, and adds that the appeal to what the apostles spoke does not prove the writer was not one of them: he speaks of what is past, and may include himself while naming the apostles collectively. wesleyan-arminian Wesley presses that further and finds proof inside the sentence: he does not exempt himself from the number of apostles, for in the next verse he says they told you, not us. reformed Calvin observes what the arrangement does — to a most ancient prophecy he adds the admonitions of the apostles, whose memory was recent — and thinks it makes little difference whether the verb is read as statement or exhortation, since either way the readers are fortified by the prediction. Robertson notes the verb stands here as an imperative where the parallel epistle has an infinitive, and that the holy prophets named there are absent. Gill says the address distinguishes them from the false teachers, so they should not be surprised at what was foretold. What the last time means divides them. Clarke takes it for the conclusion of the Jewish polity; Calvin for that state in which the renewed condition of the Church received a fixed form until the end of the world, beginning at the first coming of Christ — and he describes the scoffers as men inebriated with a profane contempt of God, in whose hearts no dread of judgment exists and therefore no hope of eternal life, adding that his own world was full of them, madly scoffing at the whole doctrine of religion as fabulous.

The charge of separation is where the readings come apart. Gill takes it of separating from the saints: not from the openly profane, which is commendable, nor from superstition, which would have been right, but from the pure worship and discipline of God’s house and from the ministers of the word, making divisions out of pride and vain glory. Clarke has them leaving the true Church from an affectation of superior wisdom; Barnes, from their brethren and from the work of benevolence and truth. Calvin rejects the whole reading. That interpretation is the common one, he grants, yet it seems inconsistent with what was said before, that these men crept in stealthily and feasted with the members of the Church. The verb properly means to divide two portions by a boundary, and so to cause divisions: these are they who cause divisions. They were producing discords within the Church and not separations from it, and by continuing in it became spots and stains to its members. Robertson supplies the philology, calling the double compound a rare word used elsewhere of making logical distinctions. Wesley grants that separating is a heinous sin, but enters a caution about the word: by the church must be meant a body of living Christians, and by separating the renouncing of all religious intercourse with them, no longer joining in solemn prayer or the other public offices — and we have no more authority from Scripture to call even that schism than to call it murder. puritan-evangelical Henry makes the comparison the other way: sensual men separate from Christ and his church and join themselves to the devil, the world and the flesh by ungodly practices, and that is infinitely worse than separating from a branch of the visible church over opinions or the modes of outward government and worship. On the last clause they agree: the word rendered sensual means the merely animal man, opposed to the spiritual; and Calvin adds that in the degenerate nature derived from Adam there is nothing but what is gross and earthly, so no part of us aspires to God until we are renewed by his Spirit.
20:
The counter-charge to the indictment is a building, and the metaphor is worked hard. grammatical-historical Barnes reads it as a call to agency: they were to build up themselves, as moral and responsible agents; dependent as we are, and as all persons with correct views feel themselves to be, it is proper to do the work of religion as if we had ample power of our own. He takes the most holy faith for the system of religion founded on faith, in whose doctrines and duties they were to establish themselves. wesleyan-arminian Clarke names the foundation more narrowly, the Gospel and the writings of the apostles, on which all expectation is founded, Christ their sum and substance being the one from whom grace is sought. Wesley calls it a faith than which none can be more holy in itself or more conducive to exalted holiness, and notices the architecture: the Father, the Son and the Spirit are all named across these two verses, and with them faith, love and hope. reformed Calvin raises the difficulty the metaphor creates. Since the whole perfection of man consists in faith, it may seem strange to be told to build another building upon it, as though faith were only a beginning. He offers three ways out: that men build on faith when love is added; that faith rises as a building through its daily progress; or, which he prefers, that faith stands here for the doctrine believed. And he proposes to render the pronoun one another rather than yourselves, as it means elsewhere, making the whole passage a series of mutual duties — building one another on the holy doctrine, keeping one another in the love of God. Robertson notes the superlative is a true one, not merely intensive, and that praying in the Holy Spirit is named as the way the building is done.

Prayer and perseverance are treated together. Clarke insists that prayer not sent up under the influence of the Holy Ghost is never likely to reach heaven. Calvin makes it a doctrine of dependence: the way of persevering is to be endued with the power of God, so whenever the constancy of faith is in question we must flee to prayer; and since we commonly pray formally, the Spirit is named, our sloth and the coldness of our flesh being such that no one prays aright unless roused by him. Robertson marks a tension the chapter has been building toward: in the opening verse the readers are said to be kept, and here they are commanded to keep themselves, the two standing together as elsewhere in the New Testament. What the love of God means there is the last question. Barnes decides it from the imperative: the phrase might mean God’s love to us or ours to him, but the former cannot be the sense, since that is a point over which we have no control and could not be enjoined. Gill will not choose, offering both the favour with which God loves his people, to be set before us and meditated on, and a second sense in which the words may be rendered preserve yourselves by the love of God — a stronghold against Satan’s temptations, the snares of the world and the demands of the flesh. Calvin makes love the guardian and ruler of life, not opposed to the grace of God but the right course of our calling. On the closing clause two witnesses from opposite schools converge. Clarke insists that though they must build and pray and keep themselves, this cannot merit heaven, and after all their diligence they must look for the mercy of Christ to bring them to eternal life; Calvin says the same, that we are not to hope for eternal life except through that mercy, since Christ will judge by no other rule than the gratuitous benefit of the redemption he obtained.
22:
The closing charge is the least secure text in the epistle, and all say so. wesleyan-arminian Clarke reports the manuscripts and versions offering rebuke after having judged them, or rebuke those that differ, or convince some that are wavering, and concludes that these two verses are all confusion, that it is extremely difficult to know what the original was, and that the received reading is as likely as any. grammatical-historical Robertson says the same: some copies read refute in place of have mercy, and the participle may accordingly mean doubters or disputers, so the text is in much confusion. reformed Gill notes the reading reprove in the Alexandrian copy and in two of the versions. Calvin knows the old translation, rebuke the judged, and grants it is found in many Greek copies, but judges the first meaning more suitable and the older and genuine reading; he also objects to taking the participle passively, its active sense suiting the context better. What the received text then requires is a discrimination among those to be helped. Barnes denies that any limit on compassion is intended: not that pity was to be withheld from anyone, but that a certain class needed a peculiar manner — the timid, the gentle, the unwary, not yet fallen into dangerous error, who would be more influenced by kind words than by denunciation. To make such a distinction, without any difference in the desire for their salvation, he calls one of the highest qualifications for one who would save souls, since the young and delicate need other treatment than the rough and hardened. Calvin says the same: the meek and teachable are to be treated with kindness as objects of pity, the perverse corrected with more severity — and since asperity is almost hateful, he excuses it on the ground of necessity, for those who will not follow good counsel willingly cannot otherwise be saved.

What the fear is divides them squarely. Barnes takes it of the arguments used: appeals adapted to produce fear, drawn from the danger of the persons themselves, since while one class is won by mild persuasion another is roused only by the terrors of the law. Gill takes it the same way and names the means — sharp admonition, the judgments of God denounced, church censure inflicted in a terrible manner, the terrors of hell declared. Calvin reports that most agree with them, then dissents: what follows favours another view, that fear means the care with which such men are to be handled, since snatching a thing out of the fire is done carefully lest the rescuer be burnt, and the infected garment points the same way. Robertson agrees, glossing it as fear of the contagion of sin while we are rescuing them, and Wesley builds a rule of pastoral practice on it: watch over others as well as yourselves, deeply convince some, snatch others with a swift and strong hand out of the fire, show compassion on others more gently, though still with a jealous fear lest you be infected with the disease you endeavour to cure — loving the sinners while retaining the utmost abhorrence of their sins. Clarke adopts that note as the probable sense of the passage. On the garment Barnes canvasses the plague, the ceremonial defilement of those who touched the dead, and leprosy, and draws the same caution: while we endeavour to save the sinner we cannot too deeply loathe his sin, and not a few have been corrupted in attempting to reform the polluted. Calvin generalises it: the faithful are to beware not only of contact with vices but of everything that borders on them, hating not only the flesh but the garment which contact has infected, so that all the preparations and accessories of evil are cut off.
24:
The epistle closes where it opened, on the keeping of the saints. reformed Calvin says the writer closes with praise to God to show that our exhortations and labours can do nothing except through the power of God accompanying them; and he notes a variant, some copies reading them for you — meaning it is your duty to endeavour to save them but God alone who can do it — while preferring the received reading, since it looks back to the preceding verse and testifies that those the faithful were told to save could not be saved but by the power of God. Gill argues the same from the human side: the people of God are liable to fall into temptation, into sin, into error, and even into total apostasy, were it not for divine power, and they cannot keep themselves. Adam in innocence could not, nor could the angels, many of whom fell and the rest are preserved by grace; much less can sinful men, who want both skill and power. grammatical-historical Barnes notes that the word for keeping from falling occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means properly not stumbling, and reads the ascription as made in view of the dangers the letter describes: God only can keep us from falling amidst the temptations of the world, but he can, and if we trust him he will. Robertson supplies the image behind the word, a sure-footed horse that does not stumble, applied by the moralists to a good man. puritan-evangelical Henry qualifies the faultlessness: not as those who never have been faulty, but as those who, but for God’s mercy and a Saviour’s merits, might most justly have been condemned long ago. Our faults fill us with fears, doubts and sorrows, he says, but the Redeemer has undertaken that his people shall be presented faultless; and where there is no sin there will be no sorrow, where there is the perfection of holiness the perfection of joy. wesleyan-arminian Clarke catches a link the others miss: the word many copies use for faultless means without spot, an allusion back to the spotted garment of the previous verse. Wesley reads the presence of his glory as his own presence, when he is revealed in all his glory.

The last verse raises one question of substance and several of text. Gill takes the only wise God our Saviour for the Lord Jesus Christ, truly God though not to the exclusion of the Father and the Spirit, the wisdom of God and author of all wisdom, and the only Saviour of his people; Clarke reads it the same way, of him who by his blood washed us from our sins. Barnes weighs it more cautiously. The word Saviour may be applied to God as such, since he is the great Author of salvation, though commonly used of Christ; no one can certainly deny it was designed for Christ here, nor demonstrate that it was, and since everything fairly implied may be applied to God, that is the most natural interpretation. Robertson takes the same side, adding that the title is used of God eight times in the New Testament. Clarke reports that many manuscripts add by Jesus Christ our Lord after Saviour, and before all time after dominion and power, both received into the text by a critical editor; Robertson treats the latter as text and calls it, with the now and the unto all the ages that follow, as complete a statement of eternity as human language can make. Calvin analyses the four ascriptions: dominion is the right to govern, imperial authority; might the strength to effect his purpose; greatness comprises knowledge, wisdom, holiness and all that constitutes what is really magnificent; and glory is the result of these, which is why the ultimate issue is named first and afterwards the things leading to it.
